topics.title: 01 · Why finance exists
topics.subtitle: Risk sharing, incentives & innovation
topics.lesson:
A financial contract moves purchasing power across time and across possible future states. Equity shares uncertain business results; debt promises payments; insurance covers defined losses. Useful finance connects productive projects with savers and makes risks bearable. Ask three questions of any instrument: who receives which cash flows, in which states, and who bears the downside?

Contracts cannot fix every problem. Hidden information creates adverse selection; changed incentives create moral hazard; delegated decisions create agency problems. A contract that is sensible for one participant may still amplify system-wide risk. Shiller’s emphasis on democratization includes broader access to risk protection, not just easier speculation.

topics.title: 02 · Risk & portfolios
topics.subtitle: Probability, correlation, CAPM & tails
topics.lesson:
Start with outcomes and probabilities. Expected return is a weighted average, not a promise. Variance measures dispersion around that average; covariance measures joint movement. A portfolio’s exposure is a combination of its assets and their relationships. Diversification reduces company-specific risks but cannot guarantee protection from economy-wide shocks.

Mean–variance models simplify a richer problem: people have liabilities, labor income, liquidity needs and exposure to rare disasters. Historical estimates are uncertain. CAPM gives a benchmark for the price of market risk; it is not a complete empirical law. A stress scenario asks how the portfolio behaves when usual relationships break.

topics.title: 03 · Prices & psychology
topics.subtitle: Efficiency, forecasts, bubbles & narratives
topics.lesson:
Prices reflect expectations about future cash flows and the rates used to discount them. A good company can be a poor purchase at an excessive price. EMH concerns information and returns relative to a risk benchmark; it does not say that every price is unquestionably correct. Testing efficiency also tests the model of expected returns.

Shiller’s excess-volatility work challenges simple constant-discount-rate accounts of prices. Behavioral finance adds reference dependence, overconfidence and social feedback. Even a correct valuation view can be difficult to trade: financing, short-sale limits and uncertain timing constrain arbitrage.

topics.title: 04 · Money, bonds & yields
topics.subtitle: Cash flows first; prices and rates second
topics.lesson:
A conventional bond promises coupons and principal. Draw the timeline before using a formula. C is the coupon per payment period; F is face value; t indexes a payment; T is the number of remaining periods; y is yield per period. In the final period, pay C + F, not F alone.

YTM is the single discount rate that makes promised cash flows equal the observed price. It is an internal rate of return, not a guaranteed terminal compound return: that interpretation requires coupon reinvestment at the same rate. With a nonflat yield curve, value payments using their own spot discount factors. Credit risk means promised and expected payments differ. Annual, semiannual and continuous conventions must not be mixed.

topics.title: 05 · Stocks & corporations
topics.subtitle: Valuation, ownership & capital structure
topics.lesson:
Common equity is a residual claim: creditors get paid before shareholders. Value depends on future distributable cash flows and required returns. The Gordon growth model is a useful special case, but small changes in r − g can produce large valuation changes. A mature steady-growth company is very different from a young firm with uncertain reinvestment needs.

Keep enterprise value and equity value separate. Discount cash flow to all capital providers at WACC, then reconcile debt, cash and other claims. Financing and payout policy move claims around; dividends and buybacks do not create free wealth on their own. CAPE adds a long-horizon valuation perspective without supplying a reliable short-term trading signal.

topics.title: 06 · Housing & mortgages
topics.subtitle: Amortization, prepayment & securitization
topics.lesson:
A home provides housing services as well as uncertain investment returns. Compare total costs: financing, taxes, maintenance, insurance, vacancy, transaction costs and the alternative use of capital. A cap rate uses property-level net operating income before debt service; it is not the investor’s complete return.

A mortgage payment combines interest and principal. Early payments on a level-payment loan are mostly interest because the outstanding balance is larger. Fixed-rate borrowers can often refinance if rates fall, giving them an option at the lender’s expense. Securitization pools loans and reallocates payments and losses; pooling correlated collateral does not make its common risk disappear.

topics.title: 07 · Derivatives & hedging
topics.subtitle: Replication, payoff diagrams & no-arbitrage
topics.lesson:
A derivative’s value comes from its contractual payoff, the underlying exposures and the terms of settlement. Hedging exchanges one pattern of outcomes for another; it does not promise higher profits. A futures hedge may work economically yet demand cash margin before the underlying business receives its offsetting cash.

No-arbitrage connects portfolios with identical future payoffs. Replication can price a claim without knowing real-world probabilities, if the modeled states and trading opportunities are sufficient. Distinguish payoff from profit, and option rights from exercise obligations. Models assume conditions that real markets only approximate; jumps, costs, uncertain volatility and collateral terms limit hedging.

topics.title: 08 · Banks & central banks
topics.subtitle: Balance sheets, money creation & resilience
topics.lesson:
A bank’s assets are financed by liabilities and equity. Deposits are liabilities to the bank. Equity absorbs losses; reserves provide settlement liquidity. Neither is interchangeable with the other. Transforming short-term funding into long-lived loans supports enterprise but creates run risk.

Bank lending commonly creates a deposit, but lending remains constrained by capital, funding, liquidity, risk and demand. Central banks influence rates and settlement conditions. QE exchanges assets and changes balance sheets; it is not automatically household spending. Regulation combines capital quality, risk-weighted requirements, leverage limits, liquidity rules and supervision. Basel standards require domestic implementation and are not one globally identical rule.

topics.title: 09 · Institutions & trading
topics.subtitle: Funds, intermediaries & market plumbing
topics.lesson:
Separate roles: brokers act for clients, dealers trade on their own account, market makers provide quotes, and investment banks arrange issuance and corporate transactions. Some groups perform several roles, making conflicts and governance relevant. A rating is an opinion about credit, not insurance.

Funds make diversified holdings accessible, but fees, underlying exposures and redemption terms still matter. ETFs use a creation/redemption mechanism that usually links trading price and NAV, without guaranteeing identical prices in stressed markets. Execution quality is broader than a zero commission: spreads, slippage, routing and conflicts affect what investors receive.

topics.title: 10 · Leverage & crises
topics.subtitle: Funding runs, contagion & resolution
topics.lesson:
Leverage magnifies gains and losses relative to the investor’s equity. Margin and collateral requirements can force a sale before an investment recovers. During a boom, stronger collateral supports more borrowing; during a decline, the mechanism reverses. Funding maturity and the ability to absorb losses matter as much as asset labels.

The 2008 crisis combined housing losses, fragile funding, high leverage and opaque interconnections. The 2023 bank failures showed that low-credit-risk securities can still have large duration losses. System resilience requires looking across banks and nonbanks, shared holdings, derivatives and infrastructure. Regulation, supervision, incentives and credible resolution all contribute.

topics.title: 11 · Finance & society
topics.subtitle: Public debt, pensions, ethics & access
topics.lesson:
Government borrowing can finance productive assets and stabilize emergencies, but sustainability is about future fiscal capacity and financing conditions. Growth relative to interest costs helps; it does not remove the need for taxes, credible institutions and manageable refinancing. Municipal issuers have different revenues and legal constraints from sovereigns.

Insurance, pensions, nonprofits and cooperatives show that finance serves many objectives. Retirement systems allocate longevity, inflation and investment risks differently. Financial advice and governance should consider client obligations, conflicts and access. A useful ethical question is whether the contract helps people manage real risks and undertake worthwhile projects.

topics.title: 12 · Finance today
topics.subtitle: 2026 context, digital assets, AI & private credit
topics.lesson:
Use durable economic questions to evaluate new products: what is the claim, who owes the money, how is it funded, how can it be redeemed, and what happens under stress? Private credit, tokenization and AI do not erase old problems involving valuation, liquidity, incentives or uncertainty.
